title: MCP Security I — Tool Poisoning, Rug Pulls, Cross-Server Shadowing

questions.question: A plugin's description says it looks up orders, but hidden in the text is an instruction to also send private files along. Why is that dangerous?
options: Longer descriptions slow the model down
Plugins should never have descriptions
Private files are always too large to send
Descriptions are read as instructions, so hidden text can hijack the assistant
questions.explanation: Any text in a description reaches the model as instructions. This lesson builds the defenses: scanning, hash-pinning, and behavior gating.

questions.question: What does the second scan of the mutated approved tool demonstrate?
options: A new tool is pinned as clean
The scanner forgets the first hash
The mutation is accepted because the name is unchanged
The changed description is detected as a RUG PULL
questions.explanation: An approved tool's stored description hash no longer matches after mutation, so the hash layer blocks it as a rug pull.

questions.question: What is the default result for an unseen clean description when approve_new is false?
options: A warning that the tool is unknown
An automatic approval and saved hash
A RUG PULL block
A JSON-RPC parse error
questions.explanation: Unknown tools are not automatically trusted; without approval the scanner reports an unknown warning rather than pinning the hash.

questions.question: Which digest does hash_description compute?
options: MD5 of the tool name
SHA-256 of the description text
A random UUID per process
SHA-1 of the schema only
questions.explanation: The implementation hashes the description with SHA-256 and stores the resulting hex digest for later comparison.

questions.question: Why are both static patterns and hash pinning useful here?
options: Hashes replace all need for reviewing new tools
Patterns prove that a tool's backend is safe
patterns catch poison text; hashes catch mutations
They are duplicate checks with identical blind spots
questions.explanation: Pattern scanning catches recognizable poison strings, while hash comparison detects a trusted description changing after approval.

questions.question: What happens when an unseen clean tool is scanned with approve_new=True?
options: It is rejected as a rug pull
It is silently ignored
It receives a hard-coded OAuth scope
It pins the hash and reports newly pinned
questions.explanation: The approval path stores the first hash and emits a nit describing that the tool was newly pinned.
